title: Where the sun sets
hook: your sunset point slides along the horizon through the year

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hour so many traditions mark. Your line was watch it go. Did you catch the sunset? Day one hundred forty-nine.

Where, exactly, does the sun set from your home? Behind which building, which tree, which hill? "In the west" is the usual answer. True, roughly. But watch from the same spot every evening for a year, and you'd see what the builders of Stonehenge tracked with care. The sunset point doesn't stay put. It walks. Slowly, all year, back and forth along the horizon. Today's practice is where the sun sets.
screen: `BEHIND WHICH TREE?` → `NOT THE SAME PLACE TWICE.` → `WHERE THE SUN SETS.`

segments.voice: Here's why. The Earth is tilted, a bit more than twenty-three degrees, and as it circles the sun, that tilt makes the sun's path across our sky shift through the year. On two days, the equinoxes in March and September, the sun sets almost exactly due west. After the March equinox, if you live in the northern half of the world, the sunset point creeps north, day after day, until the June solstice, its farthest point. There it seems to pause, then turns back south, passing west again in September, all the way to its southern limit at the December solstice. In the southern half of the world, it's the mirror image. At the latitude of New York or Madrid, the whole swing is wide, roughly sixty degrees of horizon. Solstice comes from Latin words meaning the sun stands still, because at the turning points it seems to linger for a few days before heading back. People have watched this for thousands of years, with great care. Stonehenge, in England, is lined up with the midsummer sunrise and the midwinter sunset. And in New York City, twice a year, the setting sun lines up exactly with the cross streets, flooding them with light, and crowds gather to watch; the astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson gave it the name Manhattanhenge. There's something steadying in it. The sunset point is always moving, and always coming back. Change and return, in one slow sweep.
screen: `THE TILT OF THE EARTH.` · `DUE WEST AT THE EQUINOXES.` · `SOLSTICE: THE SUN STANDS STILL.` · `STONEHENGE TO MANHATTANHENGE.` · then, large: `IT MOVES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: prepare to note today's sunset point. Settle, and breathe. Picture the place you watched from yesterday, or a window facing roughly west. Picture the horizon there: a roofline, a tree, a pole, a hill. Pick one landmark. Tonight, you'll notice where the sun goes down against it. In a few weeks, look again from the same spot. For now, just picture the slow walk of the light. The bell holds the time.
Where the sun sets. A point that slides along your horizon all year, north and south, and always comes back. Today's word.
Your line: it moves. Tonight, note today's sunset point against one landmark, and write it down or take one photo. We'll come back to it. Day one hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Sky watchers, farmers and photographers track where the sun sets against a fixed landmark through the year, and some ancient monuments, like Stonehenge, are aligned with solstice sunrises and sunsets.
